name: Freya Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm second flute in the city opera orchestra. We play in the pit, under the stage, so the audience mostly sees the tops of our heads. Rehearsals are usually ten till one, then a show at half seven four nights a week in season. On Saturday mornings I teach flute at the Lindenhof Music School, mostly teenagers preparing for exams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is the moment the lights go down and two hundred people go quiet at once. The worst is my back after a four-hour Wagner, folded into a pit chair. People think an opera pit is glamorous, but it's mostly counting bars in the dark and trying not to sneeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that, then. I don't get very worked up about technology news. I'd probably just mention it at the coffee break and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes for me. Nobody's going to replace a pit orchestra with software for a few small savings. Even the box office already uses some automatic booking, and it hasn't touched us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Contract renewal is next spring and I'd expect it to go through as normal. Jonas and I are saving for a bigger flat, and we'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved isn't the right word, because I wasn't worried to begin with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your partner's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas is an accountant at a mid-sized firm. In this picture his software gets a bit smarter and he finishes month-end a day earlier. My partner Jonas would finally get home before nine at the end of each month, and that's all the change I'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The opera's funding. The city cut the arts budget a little this year, and they're talking about a shorter season. That's nothing to do with AI, but it's there in the background.

I'd point out I don't get very **worked up** about technology news anyway.
think: Nobody replaces a **pit orchestra** with software for a few small savings.
The box office already uses **automatic booking**, and it hasn't touched the musicians.
do: Expect the **contract renewal** next spring to go through as normal.
Keep saving with Jonas for a **bigger flat**.
feel: **Calm**, because she wasn't worried to begin with.
S0.quote: My partner Jonas would finally get home before nine at the end of each month, and that's all the change I'd notice.
fieldNote: Freya's salaried **live job** feels safe to her, and she's not a technology person.
Her real background worry is **arts funding**, not AI.
She talks about Jonas's job as a **small win**, not a threat, in this picture.

steps.text: Renew the opera orchestra contract next spring as usual
Keep the monthly savings for a bigger flat with Jonas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we'll have to see how it plays out. I'd be careful not to say anything too strong. Half the orchestra would be furious and the other half wouldn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is probably fine. The bit I'd think about is Jonas, because accounting is right at the top of the list. And maybe Saturday teaching, if parents decide an app can coach their kids for exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much myself. I'd keep my two jobs and keep saving. I'd talk to Jonas about whether we should hold off on the bigger flat for a year until we see what his firm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Jonas, a little for my students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the flat. What's the actual decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got a deposit saved, and we were going to start looking in March. I'd say let's wait until next March. I'd rather rent for one more year than sign a mortgage while my partner Jonas's job is changing under him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't see what for. I play the flute, I read music on paper, and I mark my students' exam pieces by ear.

I'd avoid **strong opinions** at work, because the orchestra would split over it.
think: **Jonas's** accounting job is right at the top of the list, and maybe my Saturday teaching.
do: Keep both jobs and keep **saving** as she does now.
Push back the **flat search** by a year while Jonas's firm changes.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on behalf of Jonas and a little for her students.

fieldNote: Freya's own work is **hands-on and live**, so she sees herself as safe.

steps.text: Keep playing in the opera pit and teaching Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast for anyone to handle well, and I'd hope the government does something sensible. I wouldn't pretend to know what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Jonas's job is in real danger by 2028, and that's half our household income. The opera would probably survive, but the people who buy tickets and sponsor seasons will be losing their jobs too. If the season gets shorter, I lose pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at the opera and do my job well. We'd stop the flat plans completely and keep the deposit as a cushion. If Jonas lost his job, I'd ask Lindenhof for more teaching hours on weekday afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we have savings, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't believe a robot will sit in a pit and play second flute in my working life. Maybe I'm wrong. A robot that can breathe through a Mozart phrase the way a flautist does is not something I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Jonas talk about money if he lost his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very practically. He's the spreadsheet person, so he'd have a plan within a week. We'd live on my salary and not touch the deposit for at least a year.

I'd hope the government does something **sensible**, without pretending to know what.

A **shorter opera season** would cut my pay if ticket buyers and sponsors lose jobs.

feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, because they have savings.

fieldNote: Her mood comes from **household income**: Jonas is a likely loser in fast AGI.
She doubts **robots** will ever play in the pit, which keeps her own job feeling safe.

steps.text: Keep playing second flute and stay reliable at rehearsals
Cancel the flat purchase plans with Jonas
Hold the flat deposit untouched as an emergency fund
Ask Lindenhof for weekday afternoon flute teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, just with less fuss. I'd say five years gives people some time, and that's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still comes down to Jonas. With five years' warning, he'd have time to move into something less exposed, maybe the advisory side where clients want a person. My own job I'd still see as safe until at least 2034, probably longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd encourage Jonas to start moving now. For me, I'd keep my contract and maybe audition for principal flute somewhere, because a principal seat is harder to cut. We'd probably still buy the flat, but a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like waiting for a test result you think will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An audition is a big step for someone who likes things as they are. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the same work, just a better chair. It isn't a new career. An audition for principal flute is the only kind of change I'd actually choose for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a smaller flat look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two bedrooms instead of three, further from the centre. We'd keep a bigger cushion in the bank instead of a spare room.

steps.text: Prepare and audition for a principal flute seat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we'll manage. I'd probably not post anything at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years takes me to thirty-seven, Jonas to forty. That's enough time for him to change direction without panic. My job will look much the same, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the three-bedroom flat as planned, maybe a year later. I'd keep my contract and the Saturday teaching. And I'd let Jonas lead on what he does, since it's his career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Uneasy in the background, but mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Children in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. That's part of why we want the third bedroom. With ten years of warning, I'd still want the third bedroom, because a baby isn't something I'd postpone over a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Lindenhof made us use one for marking, I'd learn it. But I wouldn't go looking.

I probably wouldn't **post anything** about it online at all.

My **job** will look much the same, I think.

Keep the **opera contract** and Saturday teaching, and let Jonas lead on his own career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of Jonas. What would help is time for people like him to retrain, with some support while they do it, and steady funding for the opera so the season doesn't shrink.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you covered it. Maybe the arts funding, which isn't AI at all but worries me more some days.
